transcript.text: The oldest bag preserved in the history is from the Tyroline Iceman.
This nickname was given to a well-preserved natural mummy.
The man reportedly lived between 3,400 and 3,100 BC.
In the 14th and 15th centuries, bags were caught the purses, exclusively carried coins.
These purses were essential, as the pockets in clothing were not developed just yet.
In the 14th century and without the pockets in clothing, a purse was attached to the strains
of from the waste.
From the 16th century onward, priests often wore the purses, a hook with chains to which
small things could be attached, such as keys, knife cases, scissors and sewing tools.
Since purses were often crafted from the precious metals, they were also considered as a symbol
of status.
The design and accessories involved in the course of centuries, but it wasn't until the
beginning of the 20th century that the handbag finally replaced it.
Facts and purses came in a variety of designs for a number of purposes, such as bags with
clasps, leather poaches.
These were all worn attached to the belt.
The introduction of pockets towards the end of the 16th century meant that man's bags
slowly disappeared in a course of 17th century.
From then on, bags belonged to almost exclusively to the women's domain.
In the 17th and 18th century, women's clothing were so large that one or two bags or pockets
could easily be heightened underneath the skirt.
Such pockets were usually worn in pairs.
One hanging from each hip hence the name thigh pockets.
Thigh pockets remained fashionable for most of the 19th century.
The dark times of the medieval age give a way to manufacturing or curious portraits on
purses.
Medieval purses were not only used as coin purses, they also were closely connected with
marriage.
As a result, they commonly showed the love stories.
Interestingly enough, this connection is deduced from connection between the handbag and
the fertility.
Bags alter to serve their uses to optimize their wearers way of life, at least such was
the case with sweety bags, which are the bags that filled with sweet smelling material.
In a time when personal hygiene was poor, sweet bags were stuffed with sweet smelling spices
to get rid of bad smelling.
For example, lavender's or perfume the balls of a cotton.
In a long run, sweet bags were also stored with clothes and the linens used for aroma therapy.
The bag continued to be highly functional and had many different nicknames and uses.
Purses were often used as decorative package for gifts, such as the money, perfume or
jewels.
Notably, towards the end of century purses became more sophisticated.
Evolving from simple draw-strain design to more innovative shapes with dynamic materials.
Summingly, texture and manufacturing attributes were the only details left to be stylized.
For instance, the 1930s saw the art deco style arrival.
This particular style specifically highlighted the abstraction, just like any time period,
which experiences new industrial materials, the bag integrates them as well as within
its design.
In its particular case, plastic and zippers were introduced to the bag.
Once the 1960s began, the bag experienced a self-expression.
As if being dynamic and versatile wasn't already a part of bag's characteristics.
The bag experienced a brave awakening, specifically colorful patterns and flower power introduced
an energy into the fabric of the bag.
The end of the 1960s saw the shoulder bag return and with it came a loss of buckles, all
of which indicated that women and their bags were ultimately fit and ready for the beginning
age of feminism.
Arning all the 1980s saw an expansion in active consumption, the bag quickly changed to accommodate
purchasing power, providing logos to indicate the priorities of the owner.
For instance, sports bags such as Nike bags match athletic shoes were most popular at
this time.
As a result, vulgar bags and even the brief case specifically featured a pocket, which
were exclusively created to hold this new invention.
